newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia c.banker sees no systemic banking crisis.
newsitem.headline: Russia c.banker sees no systemic banking crisis.

text.p: Russia's banks are not threatened by a systemic crisis, but many are in a difficult financial situation, a top central banker said on Tuesday.

"There is no danger of a systemic crisis," first deputy chairman Alexander Khandruyev told a banking conference. "Banks have the potential to maintain their current liquidity, but the situation remains difficult."

Only 35 percent of Russian banks are stable, 22 percent are experiencing initial financial problems and 24 percent are going through temporary difficulties, he said. A further three percent are showing the first signs of bankruptcy, he added.
The number of active banks had shrunk to 2,119 on July 8 from 2,132 on June 1 and 2,263 on February 1, central bank figures showed.

Commercial banks posted six trillion roubles in profit in the first half of 1996 and drew even more than this from retained profits, he said. Every fourth bank is working at a loss and the number of banks with losses is growing, he said.
Where banks had difficulties, the cause was often a risky credit policy, he said.
Overdue credits accounted for 8-10 percent of all outstanding credits and in some regions amounted to 20 percent of banks' loans, he said.

Overdue debts and interest amounted to 37.00 trillion roubles, while commercial banks' reserves against loans in the central bank were 11.70 trillion roubles, he said. The central bank's target for the reserve was 19.00 trillion roubles.
Difficulties at Russian banks, highlighted recently by a few high-profile takeovers and closures by the central bank, have revived fears of a new banking crisis.
In August 1995, Russian banks suffered from a liquidity crisis that brought the interbank credit market to a standstill from which it has never fully recovered.
The central bank recently stepped up its supervision of commercial banks, introducing tougher reserve and capital requirements.
But Khandruyev said about 50 percent of banks could not fully comply with the central bank's new requirements.
However, there were positive trends. The number of banks with low capital was falling while the number of those with large capital was growing.
Average bank capital grew 49 percent to over seven trillion roubles during the first eight months of 1996, he said. --Julie Tolkacheva, Moscow newsroom (095) 941 8520
